That's a cool picture because it almost illustrates "positive lightening".

Before I confuse everyone, your picture is traditional "negative lightening", not positive. But you can easily see where the positive strike could come from and how they are different.

Positive lightening is lightening that strikes from the "top" side of the storm cell. As the cloud builds up static energy it tends to polarize with the negative side being on the bottom and the positive side being at the top. The negative side closest to the ground can discharge much more easily and broadly as its near to the earth and has a relatively unimpeded gap.

The positive side however can't easily discharge because it is much higher and sits atop the negative side of the cloud. So it builds up much more charge before it can overcome the gap and strike the ground, because of this strikes from the top of the cloud are much stronger than normal strikes. They travel farther, they strike out a head of the storm, and they can carry around 10x the current of normal strikes. This is because it can't discharge through the negative cloud, so it must build up until it can strike out over the front or side of the cloud.

"Positive Lightening" is much more deadly than normal lightening and causes more fatalities, mainly because it reaches far ahead of the cloud so it strikes before the storm starts and people seek shelter. Also because it carries more current it can do much more damage.

It seems natural that the browser should be able to handle identity - so that you only have to authenticate yourself once with the browser and then don't have to authenticate yourself with each side.

Sadly, this hasn't happened. There is an auto-fill for passwords & personal details, but you still need to click the submit button, instead of just being automatically signed in.

A while back, Mozilla launched a product called Personas that would have enabled Firefox to handle user authentication for you. That product appears to have died too.

I have two questions: Firstly, how do you think browsers should handle identity? Secondly, why do you think this hasn't happened?
How should identity be handled in the browser?

Firstly, I agree with BBQue that it's a bad idea. Secondly, it hasn't happened because...people. It's not a technological problem. There needs to be a critical mass of service operators and browser makers agreeing to use a single authentication system. Despite this, there are some single-sign-on services available. Lots of sites let you sign in with facebook or twitter accounts, but it's far from universal.

If you want to have the identity stored in the browser, rather than authenticating off a third party, well, you sort of can, with cookies. But you would need to carry the cookies with you to every browser you wanted to use. I suppose there could be some kind of browser account sync that would do this. But you would still need to sign up to services individually initially (and set them to 'remember me').
